This is literally [b]Midnight Fight Express[/b], but with loot and the ability to play with friends.
There are too many bugs at the time of EA, especially in the [u]network code[/u] when playing in coop.
[b]6 hours[/b] in coop and you finish the main story + all sub-missions at Hardcore level.
[hr][/hr]

[h1]Main cons:[/h1]
[h2]1) Loot system is broken[/h2]
The game is built on loot, from which you create your own build. On paper: the game has a bunch of stats that roll in the items you find. In fact: the builds are tied to two aspects - [u]survivability[/u] and [u]speed[/u]. There are also separate “cards” that are modifiers/gems which you put in items to get additional bonuses (such as crit, quick reload, more accuracy, etc.)
There are 4 levels of items: [b]white[/b], [b]green[/b], [b]blue [/b]and [b]red[/b].
White/Green items drop by hundreds during the mission (for each mission you get 15-20 white-green items).
Blue item you find with a smaller chance ([strike]something like 1 blue item per 2 missions[/strike]).
Red items are ultra-rare legendaries that you drop from bosses.
What you end up with: you run a level in white/green items without any “cards” (gems/modifiers) at the end of the level, you get a blue/red item of your level (because the current mission level is equal to your equipment), you put on this “super-mega-rare” red item with a lot of bonuses/perks for the next mission and at the end of this next mission (~20 minutes of real time) you get 100 white/green items [b]with stats better than you red item[/b]. [spoiler]What are these red items for then?[/spoiler]
You cannot modify/increase level, class of an item. You can only insert "cards"(gems) into a white/green/blue item and that's if you find those "cards" too. The red item can not be changed in any way, it drops with constant large number of "cards"/"perks".

[h2]2) Worthless currency[/h2]
In the game there are 2 types of currency: 
1) first to buy items(weapon/armor)
2) second to insert "cards"(gems) in the item. 
During the mission, you get a bunch of currency + as I wrote above, you receive 100 items of white-green level. After the mission, you sell 100 of white/green items for 10000 of currency and you end up with a million currency. 
Now, you have to spend this currency, but game shop is just "empty". Inside shop you can only buy white/green item(armor and weapon) with exactly the same level as you. Let me remind you that you just received 30 of the exact same items from the previous mission for free.
In 6 hours, i never bought a single item from the shop, since same items you find during the mission [u]for free[/u] and [u]with higher stats[/u].

TLDR:- A fun looter shooter, with a lot of customisation, made by a small & active dev team. Worth full price. Good enough for ~20 hours, but it offers more if you want an end-game grind to perfect your build.

- The game is broken up into main misssions, with some randomised side missions and boss fights made available as you progress through the game; all missions can be repeated to grind for resources and specific loot. Missions can also have random modifiers to change up every mission run slightly.
- Story bits are peppered into in the main missions, in between missions, and in the home base, overall it's very light but serviceable.
- The visuals may not seem flashy and high-fidelity, but the colour-palette and art-style fit the cyber-punk aesthetic.
- The music is decent, guns sound punchy and impactful; I didn't find the sound lacking in any way.
- The game plays well with a controller, but the menu UI could be a bit more distinct and clear.
- Some maps on randomised side missions might be repeated, but the enemy is varied and the missions are over quickly enough to not be an issue.
- You can increase the difficulty in all missions for more rewards, and also increase specific loot drop chance (by paying standard currency).
- There are a lot of skills and gear to choose from, and the guns in each category feel varied enough.
- Transmog exists, and you can freely change the appearance and colour of your armour and even your guns.
- There is good build variety with all the equipment, skills and unique effects of rare gear. You can modify armour/weapons with buffs and effects and it has a small cost, though I wish it was free, to allow easy and convnenient build-crafting.
- The end-game is grindy because higher level skill card upgrades require a lot of resources, and you'll want to be chasing specific gear and skill card drops to round out your build.
- The devs seem to listen to feedback and add and change some things. The game is also updated frequently for an indie title. It's fully released and still receiving updates, so kudos to the dev team.

I bought the game at a -20% discount, but I had enough fun that I would've been fine paying full price. It may seem a bit janky at first, but it's entertaining once you get into it, and for this price you shouldn't expect AAA levels of polish. If you're intrigued by the game, you should definitely give it a try, just remember to keep a timer for 2 hours and play it within 14 days of purchase (for easy refunds).

This is a pretty middle-ground review that leans towards "recommended". 

If you are like me and love the rare twin-stick-shooter aRPG then CyberCorp is worth looking into. This is quite similar to Housemarque's "Alienation" game. It leans more into looting and "buildcraft" than Alienation did, but doesn't feel quite as good to play.

I'm going to focus primarily on feedback and gameplay-feel. Game-feel is a bit all over the place. On the one hand, shooting with the various gun types does generally feel good. Unfortunately [b]hitting things does not.[/b] Enemies do not register hits particularly well, especially powerful ones. They don't flinch, knockback is almost nonexistent, and explosions don't knock them down. They ragdoll on death and that's it. 

This bad feedback issue is at it's worst when it comes to the games novel "style meter" mechanic. It's similar to Devil May Cry's mechanic of the same name, but tied to things like active reloads, slide dodges, multi-kills, and most importantly, finishers. The higher your style (from D-S) the more leeway you get with active reloads and the less damage you need to inflict on enemies before you can perform a finisher.

This mechanic works really well at increasing the pace of combat! -but the issue is that the finishers have all the impact of watching a 4 year old smash action figures against each other. The zoomed out presentation, the lengthy and sometimes very sloppy animations just make every finisher feel like an awkward mid-combat pause and not a triumphant mini-victory.

Frankly, I think finisher animations should just be removed (but the instant kill mechanic remain), or replaced with faster, flashier ones that need more particles or visual effects to sell their importance. I would even argue for something like a Shinobi style finisher where ALL enemies at the HP threshold are killed in one finisher. This would prevent the annoying (but safe) tactic of tapping "A" over and over on a group of weak enemies so you get to stay invincible during the lengthy animation.

The game also suffers from being a looter-shooter with extremely boring end-game content. The exotic weapons are typically more hindered than helped by their gimmicks, and there's little incentive to do anything but grind the same handful of missions over and over. Some of these missions randomize enemy spawns, but most do not, and the end result is an aRPG in desperate need of some kind of endless or lengthy randomly generated dungeon.

Really fun so far. A great combo of Synthetik, Roboquest, and Ruiner. A lot of fun, high paced action, and a work in progress (so be nice to the dev team). If you follow the patch notes, you will see that the releases are frequent and pack a punch.

Still needs a lot of polish. Like a lot. 

The game starts off decent enough, but the difficulty ramps up very quickly, and it seems like the game expects you to re-run the same mission 3 to 5 times to gear up before moving on. 
Side quests are also significantly harder then the main missions of what unlocks. 

There is also some serious stability issues. 
Constantly falling through floors, getting stuck in walls, trouble walking up stairs, and the game keeps forgetting what difficulty it's on. My personal favorite is when one player can walk through a door and the other can't. Or even better when the game "Hiccups" and one player gets randomly teleported halfway through the level.

For example, I loaded up a Lv24 difficulty mission. It went form "okay" to bullet sponge central. It was absolutely not the difficulty of a lv24 run. 
After grinding through the boss, I ended up getting nearly a full set of lv 32 gear. My coop partner? He got lv 26 loot. 

The game keeps bouncing between too easy and dying in one hit, with very little in between. 

Even the Unstick button doesn't work. I've "loaded" into what I believe was the floor a few times, and the unstick button just moves my position slightly, and that's it. We still have to reload a few times. 

Considering I'm only about 4 hours into the game, and I've had to restart maps roughly 20% of the time due to extreme glitches, that's not exactly a good ratio.

Although a work in progress, this game has been a real pleasant surprise. If you like Diablo like games, this really itches a scratch for looting and shooting. Been waiting for something like this for a long time, and is well worth the price tag even in it's incomplete state, Absolutely recommend to anyone looking for an ARPG with lots of fun loot and items to play with, while stalking around in a killer robot. Excited to see where this goes.

Alien Shooter in Cyberpunk Style

I should note that the game officially released on April 22, and as of the time of writing this text—April 24—only two days have passed, so it's understandable that bugs and issues are inevitable. However, their number is  large.

As strange as it may sound, before I start criticizing the game, I want to mention that I liked its concept and how it is supposed to be played. I believe that once it is polished, it will be enjoyable. But right now, it's a mediocre title that will only appeal to fans of Alien Shooter and CyberPunk.

Let me start with the positives: the game has decent visuals and is optimized compared to many other games currently being released. There is a variety of weapons and skills, as well as the option to play cooperatively.

The game lacks voice acting—at least in English. It's clear that the developers intended to add voice acting, but so far it only exists for enemies, and not all of them at that.

In the game, you can use three types of weapons: melee, primary, and secondary. You can experiment with weapons—changing them during missions. However, the shooting feel is poor: whether you're shooting a pistol, shotgun, or submachine gun, there isn't much difference; only the model and tracers vary.

Now about skills: out of all the skills available, only a few make sense to use—namely blink and turret. My friend and I (we played both solo and cooperatively) didn't use anything else—and there was no need to. Blink is necessary for quickly closing in on an enemy or escaping from one. The turret deals some damage and distracts all enemies towards itself, allowing you to recover some health and armor. Various shields, zones, grenades, and mines are unnecessary—they're just there for variety without enhancing gameplay.

Regarding missions: locations either repeat visually or in level design. You can also often notice texture issues—they start overlapping each other or disappearing from certain angles.

At the beginning, I mentioned that the game resembles Alien Shooter in a cyberpunk style. In Alien Shooter, mobs appeared from holes in walls or floors; if they appeared differently—there was some effect. Here you can kill a boss, and suddenly a mob appears out of thin air—WTF?

Continuing with mobs: during combat, it's not always clear whether a mob has a weapon or not; the only difference is in their name and weapon type. They all look completely identical; not even all mobs are recolored.

Regarding co-op: I specifically invited my friend along to avoid saying "These problems are only happening to you." No, these problems aren't just mine; some people notice them and some don't. Back to co-op: it's generally decent but has its downsides.

First: we were occasionally knocked aside.
Second: some missions are not well-optimized for co-op. For example, we couldn't enter a capture point location together; I had to complete it alone while my friend couldn't pass through a barrier. Damage could be dealt both to him and by him. 
Third: there aren't enough missions designed for co-op; I'd like something like an endless mode—as seen in Warframe—where after a certain time you can choose to finish the mission and collect resources or risk everything for increased rewards.

The sound design is good; it sets the pace in the game, so to speak. During fights, the music really comes into its own, and during shootouts, the tempo and volume of the music change, allowing you to fully immerse yourself in the world of cyberpunk. By the way, perhaps that's why in your apartment—which also serves as the game's hub—you can choose different soundtracks from the game and re-listen to your favorites. The music truly transports you to the world of cyberpunk, which has a very positive effect on your overall mood and attitude towards the game.

The game is being developed by 20 people and in fact, what they have done is not the worst product, the game has a right to exist, but it needs to be improved: add new missions; improve the usefulness of shields, grenades and mines; or reduce their number and improve the remaining elements; fix the errors with multiplayer.

Is the game raw? - YES; 
Did you like the game? - YES; 
Do I regret spending the money? - NO; 

Rating 5 out of 10

CyberCorp is an isometric twin-stick shooter. As you can guess from the name, the game takes place in a cyberpunk world. You fight against robots, thugs with implants, and mechs to stop an evil corporation from mind-controlling people with their new chip. If you have played a looter shooter like Borderlands or Destiny before, you already know what you're getting into. The core gameplay revolves around finishing missions and getting new weapons and armor. Then you complete the same mission with increased difficulty for better loot. Rinse and repeat. In between missions you are in your safehouse, which acts as a HUB. You can upgrade your gear, watch TV, or buy new stuff from the shop while in the safehouse. The gameplay is excellent in CyberCorp. It's fast-paced and rewarding. The game encourages an aggressive playstyle. Especially melee combat is really satisfying. Customization is amazing. You can customize everything in the game. Visuals and the color of your armor or the color of your weapon. Variety is superb, and you can create cool-looking characters. The game is very short, unfortunately. If you don't grind or don't do any of the side missions, you can easily beat it in a day. Optimization is fine for the most part, but there are some frame drops here and there. The music is average, nothing special about it. Overall, CyberCorp is a great game. If you like this genre, I'm sure you'll like CyberCorp

This top-down shooter ARPG (not a roguelite) had a fair bit of fun potential, but flopped out of early access like a fish gasping for air in the boat, with bugs and a suspicious smell as though the early access time was shortened from a year to a mere eight months.  Ever see a game come out four months early because it was just in that great of shape?  Not here either, and there are issues reported years before early access even started when it was just a demo.  Expect plenty of jank and clunky action and you might have an ok time, but the game does feel rather limited, and the higher difficulty seems, well, very [i]annoying[/i] on top of those limitations.

There are only a few fairly set missions to play over and over, with fifteen mainline story missions plus about six types of "side" missions, but the bigger issue is the game basically only knows one trick: spawn constant stream of enemies in walled area until done.  There's no endgame, just replaying the same few missions hoping for new drops (which are set by mission and viewable, so you may not even have choices for where you go if you want something specific, but at least you can see that in-game) and combining upgrades to push them up tiers.  This leaves a lot of grinding and general sameyness in place of content or interesting things to actually do.

And sameyness is an issue.  The game throws a lot of enemies at you, and has a surprising library of really annoying enemies, from guys that charge a sweeping slide which can down you from off screen, large AoE stomps that drop with no warning, snipers that vanish as you hit them, annoying beam bots that track you about as fast as you move, and let's not forget one of the greatest action sins ever conceived: attacks that reverse the player's controls.  Yet, despite enemy diversity, how the fights run blurs a lot of specifics together and leaves you more frantically wearing down local annoyances than enjoying the dance of battle.  You are driven around like a kite on the wind by the mass of incoming damage/powers that feel more like relentless pestering, and you often cannot just focus down specific targets (especially troublesome when some have large regenerating shields) and just feel no real control of the field.  So often, games take us from technological supersoldier to child running around table.

In gearing, it costs special currency to apply upgrades, to remove/replace upgrades, [i]and[/i] to combine upgrades, so that special currency really obstructs you and feels like merely another grind element in place of content value.  I don't really find drop rates and currency sandbags "content", but if you have a high tolerance for that, it might feel like less of a drag, but it's definitely still a drag, and you can't just swap your build around to play differently or try out a new item, because gear changes get so expensive and combining mods to climb tiers makes it that much harder to actually have spares of things (on top of ballooning costs).  Drops already hold you back plenty, so the added special currency sandbag to even swapping mods just feels unnecessary and anti-player.  And then you get to the special-tier "exotic" gear, which comes with all its slots locked so you cannot change anything, and just get whatever random variation of affixes and cards it drops with, instead of the whole upgrade custom system that's supposed to be adding value.  So, if you have your eye on one of those later, where stats matter more, you can only grind grind grind until it finally rolls a good drop.  It's a huge grind, on probably very few--if any--mission options, in a game with few options to begin with.  Especially when the game seems to have lifted not just the poor drop value (getting a good non-exotic you can use your fancy upgrades on is downright astronomical) and currency drag from toxic live service game models, but also the [i]requirement[/i] for boss grinding.  [i]Only[/i] the story boss missions drop gear with "endgame" tier affixes.  There are only [i]three(!)[/i] story boss fights in the game that can reward such gear, and not only do they get boring fast, there's gear that just doesn't drop there, so you can never get good versions of those items.  And when only three missions drop endgame valid loot, what even does endgame mean?  Once you're looking for endgame, anywhere else you go drops trash you don't want, and you can't even auto-break down loot.

Similarly, it does some downright strange things that feel simply way beyond the appropriate scope for the game, like daily login reward milestones, daily objective "quests", and achievements that require [i]hundreds[/i] of missions.  No one should putting on such mock live-service airs for a small indie shooter with 20 missions that are basically the same.  The game wants you to be tied to it and grind forever, but there's just no game here to do that with.

If you're wondering what exactly the play has, you have two guns, a melee weapon which may have a single fairly slow two or three hit combo, an invulnerable slide on cooldown (you can shoot or take other actions during the slide), and three slots for active abilities you pick from a pool of drops.  The game's design feels like it assumes you keep one of the quick-teleport movement abilities in your actives, so you may feel more like you have two dodges and two actually pickable actives.  Gun ammo is not limited, but you have clips with an active reload mechanism, so good timing can shorten your reload and contribute to your action combo (higher combo for action spaces gets some bonuses, so it's not just for show, but it's hard to pay any attention to either since fights are extremely busy).  Actives and slide all have pretty significant cooldowns, and actives both require drops and currency to upgrade.

Finally, I bought the game as early access opened in large part because of the cute Vanquish-esque slide actions you could do all over combat.  It kind of helped with the janky action and constant enemy pestering of attacks.  Shortly into early access, the slide was put on a problematic cooldown which basically killed that whole aspect of the combat feel, leaving the slide another clunky mechanic that doesn't quite fit or work.  The only consolation offered to that negative change was that you can sacrifice a significant amount of build space (and give up on exotic items in some gear slot(s), due to their upgrade lock-out) to stack multiple copies of upgrades that are one-per-mission 2% chance reward drops from a specific mission.  Frankly, I don't really feel like it's worth playing the game without that adjustment, and something like that really shouldn't take that level of grind and significant sacrificing of options to reinstate so the action makes sense again, but there's also no real reason a player would think to even do this nonsense, for how different more freely-usable sliding feels.  So, I'm mentioning this as a tip on how the action can change from its initial appearance, even though it certainly won't reach great.

The price is pretty low, though, and the co-op seems to [i]mostly[/i] function playably ([i]finally[/i]--co-op was a terrible mess for the entirety of early access), so that might earn it some time regardless, as the co-op top-down shooter ARPG space is pretty nonexistant, but co-op requires one or two more people willing to put up with it for you.  My co-op partner would rather play other games that are more fun, and I don't blame them.  [i]Edit:[/i] Tried playing the 2025 Halloween event, and co-op was completely broken, again.

Honestly, this whole review could just say, "Frequently reverses player controls during movement-critical fights, even bosses."  That's trying to really earn that thumbs down, even without counting the bugs, garbage looting, or three-mission endgame.

CyberCorp is a stylish cyberpunk action RPG that combines twin-stick shooting with a loot-focused progression system, delivering a fast and energetic experience set in a futuristic world dominated by powerful corporations. Developed and published by Megame LLC, the game places players in the role of an operator who remotely controls combat units sent into dangerous urban warzones. This premise provides a fitting backdrop for a game built around intense firefights, equipment customization, and the constant pursuit of stronger gear.

The most impressive aspect of CyberCorp is its combat. Battles are quick, chaotic, and highly dependent on movement and positioning. Enemies attack aggressively, encouraging players to stay mobile while making full use of their weapons, abilities, and equipment bonuses. The controls feel responsive, and the isometric perspective offers a clear view of the battlefield, allowing players to react quickly to incoming threats. Every encounter becomes an opportunity to experiment with different tactics, whether focusing on raw damage output, defensive survivability, or specialized status effects.

Progression is deeply tied to the game's loot system, which serves as the core motivation for long-term play. Missions reward players with new weapons, armor pieces, modifications, and upgrades that can dramatically alter performance. The variety of gear encourages experimentation, and discovering combinations that work together effectively is one of the most satisfying parts of the experience. Rather than simply increasing numbers, many items contribute to unique build possibilities that can significantly change how combat feels. This constant cycle of collecting, upgrading, and optimizing creates an addictive gameplay loop that fans of action RPGs and looter shooters will immediately recognize.

CyberCorp's cyberpunk setting also contributes greatly to its appeal. Neon lights, futuristic architecture, advanced technology, and corporate-controlled warfare create an atmosphere that feels authentic to the genre. The environments may not always be groundbreaking in design, but they consistently reinforce the game's dystopian themes. The visual presentation balances style and functionality well, ensuring that combat remains readable even when the screen fills with enemies, effects, and projectiles.

Cooperative multiplayer adds another layer of enjoyment. Playing alongside friends makes missions more exciting and introduces opportunities for team-based strategies. Different builds can complement one another, allowing groups to tackle challenges more efficiently while enjoying the satisfaction of shared progression. The cooperative component feels like a natural extension of the game's design rather than an afterthought, and it significantly increases replay value for those who enjoy multiplayer experiences. Fortunately, solo players are not neglected, as the game remains fully playable without requiring a team.

Despite its strengths, CyberCorp does have some limitations. Mission objectives can begin to feel repetitive after extended play sessions, particularly for players focused on grinding for the best equipment. The game's indie origins are also noticeable in certain areas, including content variety and overall scale. While the core gameplay remains engaging, some players may wish for a larger selection of environments, enemies, and activities to support the lengthy progression system. These shortcomings do not undermine the experience, but they do prevent the game from reaching the same level as the biggest names in the genre.

What ultimately makes CyberCorp successful is its understanding of what makes loot-driven action games enjoyable. It delivers satisfying combat, meaningful character progression, extensive build experimentation, and a visually appealing cyberpunk setting. The game does not attempt to reinvent the genre, but instead focuses on refining familiar mechanics into a cohesive and entertaining package. Players who enjoy top-down shooters, cooperative gameplay, and the thrill of hunting for powerful equipment will likely find plenty of reasons to keep returning.

The game goes for fast-paced action, giving you the option of carrying two firearms, a sword as well up to three skills. Firearms are fairly standard - assault rifles, smgs, pistols, revolvers, DMR / sniper weapons in both physical and energy varieties. Swords are just swords, really. Weapons vary in stats such as fire rate, magazine, etc., so there is some difference even among specific categories. There is a dodge in the form of a slide with a cooldown. Unfortunately, later on you are swarmed with enemies in small arenas giving little maneuverability, so the slide dodge cooldown is felt heavily, especially with certain enemy types (haymakers come to mind). The combat is responsive, and it tries to encourage movement, but then often hems you in with tiny arenas. Still, you have options to help counteract this with various skills and abilities, and healing is a possibility through both.

Loot you find can vary in quality, coming equipped with perks (that can't be changed) that increase damage types, change health regeneration, so on. High quality loot pieces can also be fitted with cards, which essentially act as gems or runestones for sockets. They aren't particularly exciting though, usually boiling down to percent increases to things such as health, shields and damage. If you collect enough of them you can 'forge' them (upgrade them) to the next level, but the power increases are miniscule per card and often require enormous amounts of resources, thus leading to immense grinding requirements.

The campaign is short, so you'll be grinding side missions for better loot. I don't have much play time, and apparently getting an 'S' rank for a mission is a pretty rare achievement, which is crazy because the early missions aren't that hard. The scoring system is silly though, as all it cares about is comboing kills, switching weapons, using skills, and performing takedowns. It doesn't really matter all that much how much damage you take - I've had missions where I consistently almost died in each combat arena, but I still received S and S+ ranks because I just mixed up all my attacks and skill usage. That suggests to me that the devs understand that the arenas are tiny, your dodge cooldown is circumstantially high, and you're going to take damage, possibly a lot of it.

It's worth it on sale, but certainly not at full price. It's a nice break to take here and there, playing a mission or two for an hour or so.

thankfully this EA release doesn't disappoint

it is in fact a rock solid top down shooter: responsive, accurate (well depending on the stats of your used deathdealer), thight controls and lots of things to pewpew.
but then it is also quite some more: 
the describtion and trailers didn't lie...there is quite some Diablo/PoE-style content here. i mean don't expect a multi-million-dollar-project, but for the asking price i've seen quite some gear, loot, and whatnot.

you can arm your toon with a primary and secondary weapon, a melee-weapon, head- chest- and legarmor, aswell as mutliple active skills.
weapons and armor come with a) lots of stats (like pellets, range, or shield/health, shield regen, speed and whatnot), but also perks and cards. these cards (perks are pretty much cards, just locked in) work as affixes or suffixes in usual Diablo-likes. 
i've seen quite some variety both for armors and weapons.
normal things like a chance to fire multiple bullets/pellets, or an accumulating ice/freeze-effect, aswell as more "mundane" stuff like -% skill cd or +% damage absorb. 
armor and weapons (and your active skills) come in rarities, which doesn't just mean higher stats, but also a higher chance of more slotable cards (+ set perks/card). you could swap out a card/perks you don't want and change it with something else pretty much at anytime for a cost. thing kinda crafting/gem-slotting light and more accesible. 
you also find active skills in the drop pool there ain't no exp-grind or skill tree. 
you pretty much gear up your alter-ego through good'old loot hunting.
the skill variety also is already here; so far i've seen a stationary auto-turrer, multiple healing-skills (like a zone or wave), aoe-damage skills like nades or a ground-bash, aswell as a damage shield (bullets) and a dash. these also come in higher tiers, which ad boni, like reduced cd or increased duration.

you get said loot either as a reward for missions or special encounters during a run, and with a rarer chance pretty much from every destroyable box or plain enemy drops. 

there is a full on campaign-mode to boot, aswell as sorta side-missions, think side-jobs like killing a specific boss, or zone-control, etc. . each coming also with 3 difficulties, which also come with their very own modifiers.
each mission (so far) can be repeated when and as many times as you like.

again: system and gameplay wise the release is rock solid. 

and frankly there's very little in the way of sci-fi or cyberpunk Diablo-likes, beeing it pure twin stick shooters or not. thankfully this isn't just banking on it is scenario but also providing quite some real looter-shooter content.
combat also flows quite well, with a fluid switch between melee and your 2 weapons aswell as the different skills; low hp enemies can be finished (keybord "F") which seems to net a higher chance of either currency loot or health pickups, there is a mild active reload (i'm old and i rarely miss a timing here, whereas i hate this mechanic usualy in faster paced games), aswell as you standart dodge/dash and a "combo"-rating and thankfully no ammo-pickup-system; ammo is managed only via your reload and you can't run out of ammo.
nigh every level i played until know also had hidden areas or rooms, either beeing accesible through small enviromental puzzles or hidden paths, which usualy lead to more loot-oppertunity.

the plot presentation is what you'd expect for a game in this price tier; apart from the animated intro it is mostly ingame cutscenes or 2D art (but it is pretty nice to look at).
the game ain't no CP2077 by a long shot, but it hits the genre vibe quite well. the screenshots and trailer(s) are very accurate. i very much dig the vibe and look, but art will always be a matter of taste. didn't run into any noticable technical issues; some minor grafical glitches on some small tiny texture in the backround (but very rare).

the OST bangs. there is quite some tracks here and pretty much all of em hit the nail on the head. more chill beats building up to Arasake-Tower-rushing bpm will always be a dopamine-hit.

you also get the fluff. your base is an apartmant. every menue is also represented in the apartment. your inventory is your armor-stand and workshop table, the map is a 3D hologram in your apartment, etc. . you can sit on a couch and watch the TV screen or look down from your balcony. the initial Titel-screen (very pretty) is a nice hint that someone at Megame likes the genre (Cyberpunk that is). 

if you can manage your expectations and understand the price-range, this is a very solid recommend.
it is fun, it is quite addicting especialy somewhat later when the lootable opens up more; it looks pretty, runs well, sounds banger and we need more game like this and less games with a "rogue"-tag to be frank.

all the game needs is more content and more exposure.
